title: Investigate shared CPU/GPU work-queue strategy for maximum decoder throughput
description:
Investigate the scheduling strategy that keeps a single GPU busy without host-thread contention, and produce a reusable recommendation for BCJR, LDPC BP, BCH syndrome, and future GPU backends.

## Background

Current GPU BCJR support proves kernel feasibility, but the host-side scheduling model is still unresolved. In the current product-code path, `run_product_frame_parallel()` creates one decoder per Rayon worker via `map_init`, and `TurboDecoder::new()` creates a `GpuBcjrBatch` per decoder instance when GPU BCJR is enabled. `GpuBcjrBatch::decode_batch()` currently launches on the default HIP stream and then calls `hipDeviceSynchronize()`. That combination is likely to serialize or contend if many CPU threads submit GPU work directly.

The open design question is how multiple CPU threads should cooperate to maximize total throughput: enough CPU parallelism to keep the GPU fed, but not so much direct submission that the GPU becomes bottlenecked by stream contention, synchronization, or tiny launches. The answer should be a shared runtime strategy usable by BCJR, LDPC BP, BCH syndrome evaluation, and future GPU kernels rather than a one-off path for a single decoder.

## Success Criteria

- [ ] Profiling artifacts compare at least two host scheduling models for GPU work submission: direct per-thread submission versus a shared GPU scheduler with bounded queueing and batch coalescing.
- [ ] Measurements cover at least BCJR batch decode and one additional GPU-oriented workload candidate (LDPC BP or BCH syndrome), with sweeps over CPU thread count, batch size, and stream count.
- [ ] Results break wall-clock time into meaningful phases where possible: CPU preparation, host-to-device transfer, kernel execution, device-to-host transfer, synchronization/waiting, and postprocessing.
- [ ] The investigation states whether the current default-stream plus `hipDeviceSynchronize()` design materially serializes multi-threaded submission, and quantifies the effect on throughput.
- [ ] The final recommendation specifies a reusable scheduling model for shared GPU backends, including the preferred ownership model for GPU submission, queue/backpressure policy, batching granularity, stream usage, and completion signaling.
- [ ] The recommendation explicitly states how CPU work should be partitioned between frame generation/preparation, GPU submission, and postprocessing so that CPU threads feed the GPU without contending on it.

## Notes

Ideas and hypotheses from current investigation:

- The current risky pattern is `worker thread -> decoder instance -> GPU launch -> global sync`.
- A likely better pattern is `CPU prep workers -> bounded queue -> shared GPU scheduler -> small fixed set of streams -> completion events/results`.
- CPU threads should prepare frames, LLRs, and batch inputs in parallel, but only a small GPU-owner layer should touch HIP submission.
- The GPU path should prefer async H2D, kernel launch, and D2H with stream/event synchronization instead of full-device synchronization in the hot path.
- Throughput should be profiled at three levels: isolated GPU microbench, end-to-end decoder/campaign path, and GPU timeline overlap/idle-gap analysis.
- Useful metrics include decodes per second, effective batch-size histogram, queue depth, GPU idle gaps, time spent waiting in synchronization, and throughput versus CPU thread count.
- The output of this issue should inform issue `37e0b235` (GPU LDPC BP decoder) and future GPU backend work, while also being applicable to the existing BCJR path and BCH syndrome batching.
